what_its_for: Amiodarone is used to treat serious irregular heartbeats (called arrhythmias), including a very fast or chaotic heartbeat. It helps your heart beat in a normal, steady rhythm. This medicine is usually prescribed when other heart rhythm medicines have not worked or cannot be used.
how_to_take: Take amiodarone by mouth with or without food, but try to take it the same way each time. Swallow the tablet whole with a full glass of water. Taking it with food may help reduce stomach upset. Take it at the same time each day to help you remember. Do not crush or chew the tablets unless your doctor tells you it is okay.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your heart condition and how your body responds to the medicine. A common starting dose for adults is 800 to 1600 mg per day taken in divided doses for the first one to three weeks. After that, your doctor will usually lower your dose to a maintenance dose, often 100 to 400 mg once a day. Always follow your doctor's exact instructions and never change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at your regular scheduled time. Do NOT take two doses at the same time to make up for the one you missed. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist for guidance.
storage: Store amiodarone tablets at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C and 25°C). Keep it away from heat, direct light, and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Do not use the medicine after the expiration date printed on the label.
what_to_avoid: Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice while taking this medicine, as it can increase the amount of amiodarone in your blood and raise the risk of side effects. Limit your time in the sun and wear sunscreen and protective clothing, because amiodarone can make your skin much more sensitive to sunlight and may cause a blue-gray skin discoloration over time. Avoid starting any new medicines, including over-the-counter drugs, vitamins, or herbal supplements, without first checking with your doctor or pharmacist, because many medicines can interact with amiodarone. Avoid drinking large amounts of alcohol.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: new or worsening shortness of breath or difficulty breathing, chest pain, a very slow or irregular heartbeat, coughing up blood, vision changes or blurred vision, unusual weight gain or swelling in your legs or feet, dizziness or fainting, numbness or tingling in your hands or feet, unusual muscle weakness, yellowing of your skin or eyes (signs of liver problems), or a fever with cough. Also call your doctor if you notice a blue-gray skin color, increased sensitivity to sunlight, or any side effects that worry you.
when_it_works: Amiodarone takes time to build up in your body and may take several weeks to months before you feel the full benefit. Some people begin to notice their heart rhythm improving within a few days to weeks. Because it takes a long time to work fully, it is very important to keep taking it exactly as prescribed, even if you feel well. Do not stop taking it without talking to your doctor first.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Amiodarone can harm an unborn baby and passes into breast milk. Tell your doctor right away if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. Older adults: Older patients may be more sensitive to the side effects of this medicine, especially thyroid problems, lung problems, and falls due to dizziness. Thyroid disease: Amiodarone contains iodine and can cause your thyroid to become overactive or underactive. Your doctor will check your thyroid with regular blood tests. Kidney or liver problems: Tell your doctor if you have kidney or liver disease, as this may affect how your body handles the medicine. Children: Use in children should only be under the close supervision of a specialist.
